Supreme Court Justices Elena Kagan and Amy Coney Barrett testified before a House committee last week, an unusual appearance, asking Congress for close to 230 million dollars in added security funding. Justice Barrett described a swatting incident at her own home. The court says threats against federal judges have topped 370 so far this fiscal year, which tells you something about the temperature of the moment beyond just the war and the Fed.

ANDREW: That oil and rate pressure runs straight into home lending, so let's stay right there. It was a mixed but generally upward week for mortgage rates. Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the thirty-year fixed at 6.55 percent, up from 6.49 percent the week before, the second straight weekly increase. The Mortgage Bankers Association's own survey, for the week ending July 10th, had the average even higher, at 6.65 percent, the highest reading since August of last year. Applications fell 2.7 percent as a result, with purchase applications down 7 percent, though refinancing actually rose 4 percent as some homeowners moved to lock in before rates climb further.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, a new CFPB rule takes effect tomorrow that eliminates so-called disparate-impact liability from fair lending enforcement under Regulation B. In plain terms, regulators will no longer be able to bring fair-lending cases based purely on statistical outcomes, only on direct evidence of intentional discrimination. Lenders should note that state fair-housing laws still apply, so this doesn't eliminate their exposure entirely, just narrows the federal standard.

ANDREW: Separately, HousingWire has reported that the median home sale price hit a record 440,600 dollars in June, the 36th straight month of gains. And the ROAD to Housing Act, which became law earlier this year, is still waiting on HUD to issue the implementing guidance that would actually put it into effect. Freddie Mac's next weekly rate survey comes out Thursday, and given where oil and yields are sitting this morning, don't expect relief.

ANDREW: Jenny, what's happening in Jacksonville today?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at mid-90s today with the heat index pushing past 100 degrees, and scattered afternoon storms are likely as the sea breeze kicks in. Forecasters are also watching Tropical Depression Two, which formed in the Gulf over the weekend and is expected to strengthen into Tropical Storm Bertha as it tracks along the northern Gulf Coast. It's not an immediate threat to us, but it's worth keeping an eye on.

JENNY: The big local story today is Mayor Donna Deegan's budget address. She presents her fiscal year twenty twenty-six to twenty-seven budget to City Council this morning at nine, and her office has previewed it as lean, with infrastructure as the top priority. Her office says she'll hold a brief media availability right after, so we should have real numbers to report by this time tomorrow.

ANDREW: Why lean this year specifically?

JENNY: It's largely about the property tax amendment on November's ballot, which would expand the homestead exemption. The city's own Council Auditor estimates that could cost Jacksonville more than 300 million dollars a year in lost revenue by the end of the decade, and that's shaping every budget conversation happening at City Hall right now, including which downtown incentives survive the hearings that follow today's address.

ANDREW: How does the property tax fight change what Council actually cuts?

JENNY: Council President Nick Howland has already flagged downtown incentive packages as the likeliest target once hearings start, since infrastructure and public safety are being protected first. We'll know more once council actually digs into line items over the coming weeks.

JENNY: Separately, a new committee starts its work today too. Howland's Financial Audit and Oversight Committee begins a 60-day review of how JEA failed to collect capacity fees it was owed, with findings due by mid-September. It replaces an earlier investigatory committee that wrapped up in June.

JENNY: One more to flag on the growth front. Four large landowners, including the developer behind Nocatee, have filed fast-tracked development applications under a new state law that lets rural land be developed as intensively as whatever's already built next door, without the standard rezoning process. The largest single parcel is more than 4,400 acres west of the Intracoastal. Separately, a rezoning hearing for the Franklin Arms property is set for Wednesday, and it's worth watching as a test case for how much pushback these fast-tracked applications get at the local level.

JENNY: And we're continuing to follow the investigation into the death of Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, the 28-year-old killed by a semi-truck last week while fleeing an ICE and Homeland Security Investigations operation on State Road 16 in St. Johns County. The Florida Highway Patrol investigation remains open, with no findings released yet, and community vigils and rallies continued through the weekend.

JENNY: Let's shift to technology, because there's a real correction to make here. Google's Gemini 3.5 Pro, which we'd expected to be widely available by now, is still not out.

ANDREW: Still not out? What happened?

JENNY: Bloomberg reported last week, citing ten current and former Google employees, that the company scrapped and rebuilt the model's base training after it kept falling short on coding performance and reliability. A widely reported July 17th launch target came and went with nothing, and Gemini 3.5 Pro remains limited to a small group of enterprise testers in Vertex AI. Alphabet shares dropped about 4 percent on the news, and prediction markets are now pointing to a release sometime between late July and mid-August.

ANDREW: That's a real opening for competitors.

JENNY: It is, and one place you can see that play out is enterprise finance. Taktile, a startup that builds AI decision-making tools for banks and insurers, just closed a 110 million dollar funding round led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Its software is already running underwriting, fraud detection and compliance checks for lenders like Mercury and Monzo, and this round is specifically earmarked to build out more autonomous, agent-based decision-making for regulated financial institutions.

JENNY: It's a reminder that while the frontier labs fight over chatbot benchmarks, a lot of the real money in AI right now is in unglamorous back-office automation.

JENNY: One more to close the loop on. Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit against OpenAI, which we told you about last week, is getting messier. Court filings detail specific allegations against OpenAI's hardware chief, Tang Tan, a 24-year Apple veteran, including that he directed job candidates to bring physical Apple hardware components to interviews and coached departing employees on how to evade Apple's exit security procedures. Apple's suit claims more than 400 former Apple employees now work at OpenAI. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and says it doesn't need anyone else's trade secrets.

ANDREW: That's a lot of former Apple employees in one building.

JENNY: It is, and it's a big part of why Apple is arguing this is pattern, not coincidence. Apple also names two former employees directly in the suit, along with OpenAI's corporate entities, and is seeking both damages and an injunction. Nobody expects this one to move quickly through the courts, but it's already reshaping how frontier labs think about hiring from rivals.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch over the next ten days: the Fed's July 28th and 29th meeting. Chair Warsh will have to weigh this weekend's oil shock against a June jobs report that came in soft, and he's doing it while an ethics review of his own vice chair plays out in public. Watch whether hike odds keep climbing as oil prices hold above 90 dollars, because that's the number that would ripple fastest into mortgage rates and everything else we've talked about this morning. And closer to home, keep an eye on Freddie Mac's Thursday rate release and whatever Mayor Deegan's budget address actually lands on this morning — both will tell us a lot about how this week shapes up.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
